title: Organisations and projects: finding your workspace
description: A warmer two-host conversation about workspaces, permissions, and keeping recordings in the right place. Second local pilot.

chapters.title: One team, several places, one login

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Welcome back to Learn, in podcast mode. Two synthetic voices, one practical question: when you switch organisations or projects in Kerberos Hub, what actually changes? Let's build a mental model, rather than read a diagram at you.

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: Start with two boundaries. An organisation is the tenant boundary: shared ownership, memberships, billing, and policy. A project separates operational resources inside that organisation. Every project belongs to exactly one organisation.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Let's invent a small security company. It monitors a warehouse and a shop, with a project for each. Please tell me this doesn't mean another set of logins. My password manager already has a full-time job.

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: Ha, fair point. One user identity can own or belong to several organisations. You don't need a new account for each project. But ownership, membership, permissions, and your selected workspace are different things. That's the distinction we'll keep coming back to.

chapters.title: A workspace is a selection, not a permission

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Wait, where does the workspace fit? We've got an organisation and a project. Is a workspace another container I need to create?

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: No. It's the organisation and project pair selected for your session, not a separate stored entity. Think of it as your current working context. Choosing it doesn't grant access. The backend still checks the organisation, project, and applicable permissions.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: So even an active organisation membership doesn't automatically let me operate every camera? And what about the roles and assignments shown in the guide?

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: Membership alone grants no capabilities. In the shared model, organisation roles administer the organisation; project roles act on project resources. An assignment grants a role at an explicit scope, with optional timing. Project roles are assigned in one project at a time. But this isn't today's live permission source.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Oh, that's worth stopping on. A useful model diagram isn't a checklist of everything that's already enforced. What should administrators actually use today?

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: Existing account roles, page and feature permissions, and endpoint-specific site, group, and camera allow-lists remain in use. Inserting a canonical role assignment isn't a supported way to grant or restrict current access. Project data isolation is implemented; per-member project entitlement through those assignments is not the same thing.

chapters.title: Create, switch, and keep the cameras put

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Let's put that into practice. The relevant controls are enabled, and I want to create an organisation. Where do I start?

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: Open the workspace menu below the Hub logo and choose Create organisation. The required name is between two and one hundred and twenty characters; company and contact details are optional. The creator becomes the primary owner and receives an active membership. Hub selects the new organisation, refreshes the session token, and reloads.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: And for a project, I first switch to the organisation where it should live. Just browsing another organisation in the menu doesn't make it active. What happens when I actually select a project?

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: Hub switches the organisation and project together. It validates access and that the project belongs to the organisation and is active, then saves the pair and returns a refreshed token. The application reloads to discard the old workspace view. This pins the selection to that session, rather than repointing other existing sessions.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: So it's a workspace selector, not a teleport for my cameras. But suppose a warehouse recording is still being analysed when I switch to the shop. Where does its result go?

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: Back to the warehouse project. Background processing follows stored source ownership. The recording, detections, and workflow results keep the source organisation and project, regardless of your later selection. Switching doesn't move resources, create memberships, or grant permissions. A different view, not a change of ownership.

chapters.title: Older recordings do not need a moving day

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Here's the part I'd worry about on an existing installation. We've got years of recordings. If we enable projects, do those recordings disappear until someone runs a migration?

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: They mustn't. Every organisation has a deterministic default project. Its identifier is the organisation identifier, its initial name is Project One, and its reserved slug is project dash one. That identity exists logically even before its metadata document is created. It's a real project, not a wildcard for all projects.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Project One. Not a wild naming choice, but I can remember it. What if an old recording has no canonical organisation or project fields, just a valid stable owner identifier?

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: Then that stable owner supplies both missing boundaries: the owner's organisation and default project. Existing non-empty canonical organisation or project values must be preserved. Creator, recipient, payer, and actor information is provenance; it mustn't replace higher-precedence ownership.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: So compatibility is something the running application does. Not something we unlock by rewriting old documents first?

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: Right. Historical unstamped resources belong in the valid owner's default project, not every new project. Backfills are optional normalization. They must not be required for visibility, isolation, authorization, or correct processing. If valid resources disappear, investigate runtime ownership resolution rather than treating a backfill as the fix.

chapters.title: The checks that save a support call

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: All right. I understand the model, but the switcher or create action is missing. Where should I look before deciding the feature is broken?

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: Check the feature flags. These controls are opt-in. An explicit organisation umbrella overrides both organisation and project controls; otherwise group and individual flags apply. Creation needs the matching switching interface. Flags control what the interface shows. They don't grant backend permissions or activate canonical role assignments.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: And if switching fails, or the application sends me back to the previous workspace? Is changing the saved project preference enough?

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: No. A proper workspace switch returns a refreshed token, and the frontend must use it. Check organisation access, active and unexpired memberships where applicable, project activity, and permissions. If resources are missing, check both workspace identifiers, canonical ownership precedence, and the default-project compatibility filter.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: One last naming trap. There's a domain field on the organisation. If I fill it in, have I configured the login domain?

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: No. That field is metadata. It doesn't create D N S records or enable domain-based login. A login domain controls the sign-in namespace; an organisation controls resource ownership and working context after sign-in. Sharing a login domain doesn't automatically put users in one organisation.

chapters.title: The mental model to take with you

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Let's land this. Three ideas to remember, and one safe next step. What should stay in my head after I close the guide?

turns.speaker: Guide
turns.text: The organisation owns. The project isolates operational resources. The workspace selects your session context. Membership isn't permission, and switching isn't moving data. Start by confirming the intended workspace and current access controls. Keep storage mode separate: compatibility is the default when unset; canonical-only needs validated coverage; legacy mode isn't a multi-project isolation contract.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: That's our second local pilot, with a little more conversation and a little less manual-reading. The linked guide has the exact endpoints, configuration, diagrams, and rollout limitations. This is an adapted explanation with synthetic voices, not a replacement for the documentation. Give the voices, pronunciation, pacing, and facts a listening review before we publish.
